Text: The module descriptor file is named {{c1::module-info.java}} and must be placed at the {{c2::root}} of the source directory.
Extra: This file is compiled into module-info.class and is processed by both the compiler and JVM runtime to enforce modular bounds.

Text: If Module A requires Module B, but B has not exported the package containing Class X, Module A will get a {{c1::compile-time}} error if it attempts to refer to X, even if X is declared {{c2::public}}.
Extra: This demonstrates strong encapsulation: the public keyword no longer grants global access across module boundaries.

Text: To allow Spring or Hibernate to reflectively inspect private fields, you must use the {{c1::opens}} directive, whereas exposing public APIs for standard compilation requires the {{c2::exports}} directive.
Extra: exports allows compilation and runtime usage of public types. "opens" allows runtime reflection only (including deep reflection on private fields) but forbids compilation.

Text: All classes loaded from the Classpath (instead of the Module Path) are placed in the {{c1::Unnamed Module}}, which automatically exports all its packages.
Extra: While it exports everything, named modules cannot declare requires on the unnamed module because it has no name.

Text: If a legacy JAR is placed on the Module Path, it becomes an {{c1::Automatic Module}} and receives a name derived from its {{c2::JAR filename}} or manifest header.
Extra: This serves as a migration bridge, allowing modular code to require legacy libraries.

Text: Unlike Maven dependencies, the Java Module System strictly prohibits {{c1::cyclic dependencies}} at compile-time and runtime.
Extra: This enforces clean software architecture and guarantees a deterministic module initialization order.
